My main question is about the escape hatch. Every no-code builder works great for the first 80% and then hits a wall where you need custom logic, a weird integration, or a performance fix. Can I export the app as real code (and if so, is it code a human would want to maintain), or am I locked into your runtime? Likewise, can I self-host, or at least get my data out in a clean format? That's the difference between "I'll prototype here" and "I'll build my business on this."

Pricing is the other thing I'd want to understand before committing. Per-seat, per-app, and usage-based models all have ugly failure modes once something succeeds. If a side project gets popular, does my bill jump 10x overnight? A clear answer on that, plus a roadmap for permissions and audit logging, would go a long way toward convincing teams to use this for internal tools. Good luck, and I'll be trying it this weekend.

The part of this debate that gets lost is that the 30% was never really a payment processing fee. Card processors take 2-3%, and everyone understands that's the cost of moving money. The rest is a toll for distribution, discovery, and access to a captive audience, and the reason it sticks is that on iOS there's no alternative to pay it to. If Apple were competing with other stores, 30% would have collapsed years ago, the same way Steam's cut has been under pressure from Epic's 12%. The rate itself is a symptom. The real issue is the lack of a competitive market behind it.

That said, I think people who say "just let developers use any payment system" underestimate what Apple would lose and what users might lose with it. The unified billing, easy refunds, subscription management, and family sharing all depend on Apple being in the loop. If every app handles its own payments, you get the dark-pattern cancellation flows we already see on the web. I'd like to see a world where the 30% is the price of an optional bundle of services, and developers can opt out of that bundle and take on those responsibilities themselves.

The EU's DMA has been a decent natural experiment here. Apple's response, with its core technology fee and the various tiers, shows how hard it is to get them to give up the toll rather than just rename it. I suspect the outcome that actually moves the needle is neither regulation nor lawsuits but a few big developers refusing to pay and users following them, which is exactly why Apple fights so hard over anti-steering rules.

I've run a small side project for about six years now, and the thing that made it profitable was being boring about it. It's a single-purpose tool for a niche I actually work in, hosted on one cheap VPS, with SQLite as the database and Stripe handling billing. No microservices, no growth hacking, no fundraising. My costs are around $40/month, so I broke even in the first couple of months and everything since has been margin. It doesn't make me rich (it's a few thousand a month), but it's meaningfully changed my risk tolerance at my day job.

The biggest lesson was that support and maintenance are the real product. Customers in a niche don't leave because you lack a feature; they leave because something broke and nobody answered. I answer every email within a day, keep a changelog, and write down every manual process so I can do it half-asleep. I also set a hard rule early: no custom work for individual customers unless they're willing to pay for it as a feature everyone gets. That one rule saved me from becoming an unpaid consultant.

If I were starting over, I'd charge more from day one. I underpriced for years because I was scared, and when I finally doubled the price, churn barely moved. Talk to a few customers before you launch, charge before the product feels ready, and treat the time budget as seriously as the money. A side project that eats your evenings and weekends forever isn't profitable, no matter what the Stripe dashboard says.

The thing that gets lost in most of these discussions is that "the algorithm" isn't optimizing for what you want, it's optimizing for what you do. Those diverge more than people expect. Revealed preference (I lingered on this outrage post for 8 seconds) is a very different signal from reflective preference (I'd rather not see this at all). Engagement metrics can only measure the former, so the system learns to serve the version of you that's most easily captured, not the version you'd endorse on a good day.

What makes this hard to fix is that the obvious remedies have their own problems. Chronological feeds sound great until you follow 500 accounts and the loudest, most prolific posters dominate. Explicit controls like "not interested" buttons are underused because they're friction, and the people who use them are a biased sample anyway. Surveys ("did this feel worth your time?") are probably the most promising signal, but they're sparse and noisy, and platforms have little incentive to weight them over metrics that directly track ad impressions.

I think the more interesting long-term direction is decoupling the ranking layer from the platform, so users can pick or even write their own ranking function over a shared content graph. Bluesky's custom feeds are an early, imperfect version of this. It doesn't solve the incentive problem, but it at least changes who gets to decide what "good" means, and lets the market for feed quality exist at all.

The part that bothers me isn't that Copilot can regurgitate GPL code verbatim, it's that the burden of detecting it falls entirely on the user. The "duplicate detection" filter only catches matches above a certain length threshold, and it's opt-in in a lot of configurations. So you end up with a tool that's trained on copyleft code, occasionally emits it with the license header stripped, and then tells you the output is yours to ship. If a human contractor did that, we'd call it a compliance incident, not a productivity gain.

The legal question is also genuinely unsettled, which is the worst place to be if you're a company with lawyers. Fair use arguments for training are one thing, but verbatim output is a different fact pattern, and most of the case law people cite was written for very different technology. I'd bet plenty of codebases already contain snippets nobody knows the provenance of, and the discovery process in a future lawsuit is going to be unpleasant for someone.

Practically, what I've seen teams do is turn on the public-code blocking setting, run a license scanner like ScanCode or FOSSA in CI, and treat any large, suspiciously polished block of generated code as something to review the way you'd review a vendored dependency. It's not perfect, but it's a lot better than assuming the tool has done the diligence for you.

Been doing this for about four years now, and the thing nobody told me is that the product is maybe 30% of the job. I spent the first year polishing features nobody asked for, and the second year realizing that the three customers who actually paid me were all asking for the same boring thing: better CSV import. Once I just built that, revenue doubled. Talk to your users before you write the clever thing.

The other piece is that solo doesn't have to mean alone-alone. I pay a bookkeeper and a part-time contractor for support overflow, and it's the best money I spend. The trap is thinking every hour you don't code is wasted. Some of my best weeks were ones where I shipped nothing and just answered emails and fixed a pricing page. Also, boring stack. I run it on one Postgres box and a single Rails app, and I sleep fine.

Not saying it's easy. Some months are rough and the isolation gets to you. But I'd take it over a job where I can't ship a fix without three approvals.

I've been running a solo SaaS for about four years now, and the biggest lesson is that the hard part was never the code. Building the product took maybe three months. Finding the ten people who would actually pay for it, and then figuring out why the next ten wouldn't, took the other three and a half years. If you're technical, you'll be tempted to keep polishing features because that's the part you're good at and it feels like progress. Resist it. Talk to customers weekly, even when it's uncomfortable, and treat every churned account as a free consulting session.

The second thing is that boring infrastructure choices are a superpower when you're alone. I run on a single Postgres instance, one app server pair behind a load balancer, and a managed queue. No Kubernetes, no microservices. When something breaks at 2am, I'm the only one who can fix it, so I want the system to be something I can hold entirely in my head. Every clever abstraction is a future page I'll have to answer myself. Pay for managed services wherever they save you from being on call for something that isn't your core product.

Finally, be deliberate about scope and burnout. A solo founder's most limited resource isn't money, it's sustained attention. I say no to custom feature requests from anyone not on the higher tier, I automate support with good docs and a few canned responses, and I take actual weeks off with the status page and alerts set up so I'm not fully unreachable but also not constantly checking. The businesses I've seen die weren't killed by competitors, they were killed by the founder quietly running out of energy. Build something small enough that you can keep running it for ten years.

The part that gets me every time is the "we take your privacy seriously" boilerplate, followed by the details trickling out: the data was sitting in a single bucket/database with no meaningful segmentation, retention was effectively "forever," and the credentials that got popped had far more access than any one person's job required. None of that is exotic. It's the predictable outcome of treating security as a compliance checkbox rather than an engineering constraint. If your threat model doesn't include "an employee's laptop or SSO session will eventually get compromised," you don't have a threat model.

What would actually move the needle is making data hoarding a liability instead of an asset. Right now, collecting and keeping everything is nearly free, and the cost of a breach lands on the people whose data leaked, who get a year of credit monitoring and a form letter. Until the penalties scale with the volume and sensitivity of what was retained, the incentives point the wrong way. Companies delete data when keeping it costs more than losing it, and today it doesn't.

On the practical side, if you're affected: freeze your credit at all three bureaus (it's free), use unique passwords with a manager, and move off SMS for 2FA where you can. It's tedious, and it shouldn't be your job, but it's the only part of this you control.

**I raised my rates 30% last month. Here's what happened.**

I've been freelancing as a designer for four years and hadn't touched my rates in over two. I kept telling myself clients would leave, that I'd lose my steady work, that I wasn't "senior enough" yet. Then I realized I was booked solid and still struggling to cover my bills.

So I bit the bullet. I emailed all my existing clients with 60 days' notice, kept it short and professional, and didn't apologize or over-explain. For new inquiries, I simply quoted the higher number.

The result? Out of nine regular clients, two pushed back and one left. The rest said "no problem." New leads didn't blink at the higher price, and a couple of them seemed *more* confident in me because of it.

I'm now earning more while working fewer hours, which means I finally have room to take on better projects.

My takeaway: if you're consistently busy, you're probably undercharging. Raise your rates before you feel ready.

Anyone else done this recently? How did it go?

**Per-seat or usage-based pricing? Struggling to decide**

I keep going back and forth between two options:

**Per seat:** Predictable for customers and easy for finance teams to approve. But some of our heaviest users are on small teams, so we'd be undercharging the accounts that get the most value.

**Usage-based:** Aligns cost with value and scales naturally. But I worry about bill shock, harder forecasting, and a more complicated sales conversation.

I've also considered a hybrid: a base seat fee with included usage, then overages.

For those who've been through this, what did you choose, and what would you do differently? Did you ever switch models, and how did customers react?

I ran into the same failure on an M1 MacBook, and it comes down to the build picking up an x86_64 toolchain instead of the native arm64 one. This usually happens when the terminal is running under Rosetta, or when Homebrew was installed under /usr/local rather than /opt/homebrew, so the compiler and the linker end up disagreeing about architecture. The fix that worked for me was to confirm that the shell reports arm64 when you run `uname -m`, reinstall the build dependencies using the native arm64 Homebrew, and then clean out any cached build artifacts before rebuilding. If a dependency doesn't yet ship arm64 binaries, setting the architecture flags explicitly to arm64 in your environment before building should get past the linker errors.

If you can't move off the Rosetta setup for some reason, the other option is to build everything consistently as x86_64 by prefixing the build commands with `arch -x86_64`, which keeps every step on the same architecture. It's slower, but it's a reliable stopgap until the project adds proper arm64 support to its build configuration. It would also help if a maintainer could add an arm64 job to CI so this regression gets caught automatically in the future. Happy to share my full environment details if that would help narrow it down.

Ran into this same failure on my M1 and got it building by forcing the install to run under Rosetta. The root cause seems to be that one of the native dependencies only ships an x86_64 prebuilt binary, so on arm64 it tries to compile from source and chokes on the older toolchain flags. If you open your terminal via Rosetta (Get Info on Terminal.app, tick "Open using Rosetta"), delete node_modules and your lockfile cache, then reinstall and rebuild from there, it goes through fine. Just make sure you do the whole thing in that same Rosetta session, because mixing architectures between install and build will bring the error right back.

If you'd rather not run everything under Rosetta, the other thing that worked for me was installing the Homebrew versions of python and pkg-config (arm64 builds, not the ones from /usr/local) and making sure they come first in your PATH before running the build. That let it compile the dependency natively instead of falling back to the broken prebuilt. It's a bit fiddly, so I'd try the Rosetta route first, and hopefully the dependency gets proper arm64 binaries upstream so neither of these is needed.

You can't know from the idea alone, so the goal is to test it cheaply and quickly. Here's how:

**1. Define the problem, not the app.** Who has it, how often, and how much does it annoy them? Strong ideas solve a frequent, painful problem.

**2. Talk to real people.** Interview 10 to 15 potential users. Ask how they handle the problem today, not "Would you use my app?" Friends say yes to be polite. Look for people who already hack together workarounds or pay for imperfect solutions.

**3. Check the competition.** Existing competitors usually signal real demand. Ask what you'd do differently that matters to users.

**4. Test before building.** Make a landing page, a mockup, or a manual version of the service. See if people sign up, join a waitlist, or better yet, pay.

**5. Watch for commitment.** Compliments are cheap. Time, email addresses, and money are real signals.

If strangers keep asking when they can use it, you've got something. If you have to convince everyone, rethink it.

Start with web development, unless you have a specific reason not to.

Web dev gives you fast feedback. You write some HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, refresh the page, and see the result. That keeps motivation high and teaches core skills: programming fundamentals, debugging, version control, working with APIs, and deploying something real people can use.

Machine learning builds on those foundations. You'll need solid programming (usually Python), comfort with data handling, and at least basic math: linear algebra, probability, and some calculus. Jumping in too early often means copying notebooks without understanding them, which gets frustrating fast.

A good path: learn programming basics, build a couple of small web projects, then pick up Python and data analysis. From there, try an ML course like Andrew Ng's or fast.ai, and build a project that combines both, such as a simple web app that serves a model's predictions.

The exception: if you're already strong in math or statistics, or ML is your career goal, start with Python and ML directly.

Either way, build projects. That's where the learning sticks.

I've been playing with the API for a few weeks now, and what strikes me isn't that it writes correct code, because it often doesn't, but that it writes *plausible* code. It's very good at producing the shape of a solution: idiomatic variable names, the right library calls, sensible structure. Then you read it closely and find an off-by-one, or a method that doesn't exist but really ought to. That's a weirdly dangerous failure mode, because the usual cues we use to skim code for quality (formatting, naming, comments) are exactly the things it nails.

That said, I think people dismissing it on the basis of correctness are missing the more interesting use case. For boilerplate, regex, SQL joins, converting between data formats, or "how do I call this API again," I'm already faster with it than with Google plus Stack Overflow. The key is treating it like an eager junior who has read everything but run nothing. You still need to know what you're asking for and be able to verify the answer, which means it's more of a force multiplier for people who already know how to program than a replacement for them.

What I'd really like to see is it paired with an execution loop: generate, run the tests, feed the errors back, retry. Most of the bad output I've seen would get caught by a compiler or a single unit test. The model doesn't need to be right the first time if the feedback is cheap, and that feels like a much more tractable problem than making the raw model never wrong.

Most founders price based on what they'd be willing to pay, or what a competitor charges, rather than on the value delivered. Founders are usually technical, frugal, and allergic to the feeling of asking for money. So they anchor on "what would I pay for this?" and land at $19/month for something that saves a customer's team ten hours a week. The tell is that almost nobody who raises prices ever says "I wish I'd done it later." Most say they should have done it a year earlier and lost fewer customers than they feared.

The cost of underpricing is also worse than it looks. Low prices attract the most price-sensitive customers, who churn more, file more support tickets, and ask for the most custom features. They also starve you of revenue to fund support, sales, and the boring reliability work that makes a product trustworthy. A $20 product can't afford a human on the phone. A $200 product can. Low price also signals low quality to buyers who have budget, so you can lose deals to a competitor simply because you look like a toy.

The fix is mostly uncomfortable rather than clever: talk to customers about what the problem costs them, charge a meaningful fraction of that, and treat "no one has complained about the price" as evidence you're too cheap. If every prospect says yes immediately, you're leaving money on the table. Aim for a price where a noticeable minority push back, and you'll usually find you've landed near the right spot.

I've watched this happen at three different companies now, and the pattern is always the same: the founders price based on what they'd be willing to pay, which is a terrible anchor because they're the one person on earth who knows exactly how much work went into it and is also cheap because they're a founder. Your customer is a mid-level manager at a company with a budget line that already exists and a quarterly goal they need to hit. They're not comparing you to your costs, they're comparing you to the salary of the person who'd otherwise do this, or the cost of the problem not getting fixed.

The other thing is that low prices feel safe but they're actually a slow poison. At $20/month you need a ton of customers, so you need self-serve, so you need a polished onboarding, so you need support at scale, and now you've built a whole machine to sell a thing that a single $2k/month customer would've paid for with a phone call. Meanwhile the cheap customers are the ones who churn, file the most tickets, and ask for features that only matter to them. I've never heard a founder say "we raised prices and it was a mistake" but I've heard "we should've done this a year ago" a lot.

The tell that you're underpriced is simple: if nobody has ever pushed back on your price, it's too low. A healthy number of "hmm, that's more than I expected" conversations means you're probably in the right zone. If every deal closes in one call without a single negotiation, you left money on the table, and you'll find out about it eighteen months later when you can't afford to hire.

I think the framing of "replace" is where most of these discussions go wrong. What's actually happening is that the *task mix* of a junior role is shifting. The stuff we used to hand juniors as training wheels (CRUD endpoints, boilerplate, small bug fixes, writing tests for existing code) is exactly what current tools do well. So yes, the traditional on-ramp is getting narrower, and I think anyone saying otherwise is ignoring the hiring data we're already seeing. But "the on-ramp is narrower" is very different from "the profession no longer needs new entrants."

The part that worries me is the pipeline problem. Every senior engineer I know became senior by spending years making mistakes on low-stakes work, getting code review, and slowly building a mental model of why systems break. If companies stop hiring juniors because an LLM can do the junior's tasks, they save money this year and quietly stop producing the people who can judge whether the LLM's output is any good. Reviewing AI-generated code well requires precisely the judgment that comes from having written a lot of bad code yourself. Somebody has to grow that skill, and it's not clear where it gets grown if the entry-level rung disappears.

My guess is we end up with fewer, but differently-shaped, junior roles: people who are expected to be productive with these tools from day one, but who still get deliberate mentorship on debugging, reading unfamiliar code, and understanding the system underneath. The companies that figure this out will have a real advantage in five years. The ones that treat juniors as a cost line to be automated away will be bidding against everyone else for a shrinking pool of seniors.

The part that gets glossed over in these posts is that the savings usually come from two different things that get conflated: the hardware being cheaper than the cloud markup, and the company finally having to look at what it was running. I've seen a few migrations where half the bill reduction was just deleting idle staging environments, oversized RDS instances, and cross-AZ traffic nobody remembered setting up. You could have gotten much of that without leaving AWS. That said, for steady-state workloads with predictable load, the gap is real. Egress pricing alone makes some architectures indefensible once you're past a certain scale.

The cost that doesn't show up in the "we saved 70%" headline is the on-call and expertise burden. Someone has to own hardware lifecycle, firmware updates, spare parts, network design, and capacity planning a year out instead of five minutes out. If you already have a few people who've done that before, it's very manageable, and honestly kind of fun. If your team has only ever clicked through a console, budget for a painful first year and a couple of incidents you wouldn't have had on managed services.

What I'd like to see more of is the hybrid middle: keep the bursty stuff, the managed identity and DNS, and the disaster recovery in the cloud, and put the big boring always-on compute and storage on owned or colo'd hardware. It's less satisfying as a narrative than "we left the cloud," but it's usually where the math and the risk both land.

The thing that gets lost in these threads is that "cloud vs. on-prem" is usually a proxy for "did anyone on the team actually look at the bill and the architecture." We did something similar a few years back, and about half the savings came from just deleting stuff nobody remembered launching. The other half was real, but it only worked because we had two people who'd racked servers before and weren't scared of it. If you don't have that, the math changes fast.

What I'd want to know from the article is what the staffing looks like now. Hardware is cheap, but pager duty at 3am for a dead disk controller isn't, and neither is the quarter where you find out your backup restore process was never tested. Cloud pricing is absolutely a racket at scale, egress especially, but a lot of the "we saved 70%" posts leave out the salaries and the six months of migration work where you were paying for both.

That said, I think the pendulum swinging back is healthy. A whole generation of engineers learned that servers are something you rent by the hour and never thought about what a single beefy box with NVMe can do. Most companies are nowhere near needing autoscaling across three regions. If you have steady, predictable load, owning the metal is often just the sane choice.

I work adjacent to this field, and the pattern I keep seeing is that the headline result is almost never the deployment result. A model hits radiologist-level AUC on a curated retrospective dataset from three academic hospitals, and then it hits a community hospital with a different scanner vendor, different acquisition protocols, and a different patient mix, and performance quietly drops. Sometimes the model has learned the scanner, the hospital's portable-X-ray markers, or the text burned into the image rather than the pathology. The COVID-era chest X-ray papers were the most embarrassing example: a lot of them were effectively detecting which dataset an image came from.

The second problem is that "matches a radiologist on task X" is not the same as "improves care." Radiologists don't read images in isolation; they integrate history, priors, and the clinical question, and the job is mostly about the long tail of weird cases rather than the median one. Detecting a lung nodule is the easy part. The hard parts are deciding whether it matters, communicating it, and not generating a flood of false positives that add biopsies and anxiety. Few studies measure outcomes like mortality, time to treatment, or total cost, which is where the value would actually show up. Hinton's 2016 "stop training radiologists" prediction aged poorly for exactly these reasons: demand for radiologists has gone up, not down.

None of this means the technology is useless. Triage, worklist prioritization, and second-reader tools for high-volume screening look genuinely useful, and some of the segmentation and reconstruction work is quietly excellent. But the winning products so far are narrow, boring, and tightly integrated into workflow, not the "AI replaces the doctor" story. The hype hurts because it pulls funding toward flashy benchmark chasing and away from the unglamorous work: prospective trials, external validation, post-market monitoring, and figuring out how clinicians actually interact with these tools.

I worked adjacent to a radiology AI project a few years back, and the thing that never made it into the press releases was how much of the "superhuman performance" evaporated the moment you moved to a different hospital. Same model, same task, different scanner vendor or a slightly different acquisition protocol, and your AUC drops ten points. Nobody was cheating, exactly. The training data just had all these quiet correlations baked in: portable X-rays are sicker patients, certain markers or text burned into the image, the scanner model itself. The network learns whatever works, and what works in the validation split from the same institution isn't always the medicine.

The other issue is that "detects pneumonia as well as a radiologist" is a benchmark, not a clinical workflow. Radiologists aren't sitting around doing binary classification on cropped images. They're reading the history, comparing to priors, deciding what to recommend next, and talking to the referring doc. A model that flags a nodule is useful, sure, but it's maybe 5% of the job, and it often adds a false-positive review burden that eats the time it supposedly saves. Hinton's "stop training radiologists" line is the famous bad prediction, and radiology is still short-staffed a decade later.

That said, I don't think it's all hype. Triage tools for things like intracranial hemorrhage or stroke LVO actually do shave minutes off time-to-treatment, and screening mammography results look genuinely promising as a second reader. The pattern I've noticed is that the stuff that works is narrow, boring, and wired into an existing workflow, while the stuff that gets the headlines is "AI replaces doctor." Those are very different products.

The core problem is that the people who choose enterprise software are not the people who use it. The buyer is a VP or procurement committee evaluating a feature matrix, a security questionnaire, and a vendor's ability to survive a legal review. The user is some analyst who has to click through eleven screens to log an expense. Since the user has no say in the purchase, the vendor has no real incentive to make the daily experience good. You win deals by checking boxes on an RFP, so the product accretes features to satisfy checkboxes, and each one is built to the minimum needed to say "yes, we support that."

Then the incentives compound. Switching costs are enormous, so once you're in, you're in. Contracts run multi-year, data is trapped in proprietary formats, and the integrations your company spent two years building become the moat. Revenue comes from renewals and upsells, not from delight, so engineering effort goes toward whatever the largest customer demanded last quarter, producing a pile of configuration flags and custom workflows. The codebase becomes a museum of one-off requests, and every change risks breaking someone's bespoke setup, so nothing gets cleaned up.

The final piece is that "good enough to not get churned" is a much lower bar than "good." Consumer products die when they're annoying, because users leave. Enterprise products survive being annoying for decades because leaving costs a fortune and the person who'd have to champion the migration is the same person who signed the original contract. The few exceptions tend to be tools that grew bottom-up, where individual engineers adopted them first and the procurement process came later to rubber-stamp it.

The thing people miss is that the person who buys enterprise software is almost never the person who uses it. The buyer is a VP or a procurement committee who cares about a checklist: SSO, audit logs, SOC2, 40 integrations, "configurable workflows". The user is some poor ops person who has to click through 9 screens to do what should take one. So the vendor optimizes for the checklist and the demo, not for the guy who has to live in it 8 hours a day. Nobody in the sales cycle ever asks the end user anything, and when they do it's after the contract is signed.

Then you add the fact that once you're in, switching costs are brutal. Data migration, retraining, re-doing every integration, and the 3 people who understand the weird customizations left in 2019. So the vendor doesn't actually need to be good, they just need to be not-bad-enough-to-leave. Renewal rates stay at 95% and the product team figures why bother fixing the UX when roadmap is all driven by whatever the biggest customer's lawyer asked for last quarter. Every feature is a one-off for a specific deal, so you end up with a giant pile of settings that interact in ways nobody understands.

Also the good engineers mostly go work somewhere else, because it's hard to get excited about building a Jira plugin for compliance reporting. Not saying everyone there is bad, I've worked with some great people at these places, but the incentives just don't reward taste. Anyway that's my theory, I'm sure I'm missing stuff.

I think the underlying problem isn't that people hate paying, it's that the subscription model has been applied to apps where the ongoing cost to the developer is basically zero. A weather app that pulls from a free API, a habit tracker that stores everything locally, a QR scanner, a flashlight. These get priced at $4.99/week or $39.99/year because the developer saw that recurring revenue is worth more to investors and to App Store ranking than a one-time sale. Meanwhile the user is expected to track a dozen small charges they signed up for and forgot about. I've done an audit of my own App Store subscriptions twice and found things I hadn't opened in over a year each time.

The dark patterns make it worse. Free trials that default to the most expensive annual plan, paywalls with a tiny gray X, "Continue" buttons that actually start the billing, and cancellation flows that require you to go hunting through iOS settings rather than the app itself. Apple's system for managing subscriptions is decent, but the apps have clearly optimized around the assumption that most people won't use it. The result is that I now reflexively delete any app that shows me a paywall before I've gotten any value out of it, which probably means I'm missing some good software.

The apps I'm happy to pay for are the ones where the cost is obvious: sync servers, storage, ongoing content, or real server-side compute. Those I'll subscribe to without complaint. For everything else, I'd much rather pay $15 once and get updates for a year, or pay for major versions like we used to. Some indie developers are doing this (Pixelmator, Things, a few others), and it seems to work for them. I wish Apple made that model easier, with paid upgrades or something similar, instead of pushing everyone toward recurring billing as the only sustainable path.

- You write regularly for work (emails, reports, marketing copy, documentation) and time is money.

- You write occasionally. Free tiers from the major assistants handle most casual needs.

Web dev first, honestly. Not because ML is too hard, but because you'll get stuff on screen way faster and that keeps you motivated. You learn how to code, debug, use git, read docs, deal with APIs. All of that carries over to ML anyway.

ML has a lot of math and data wrangling that can feel like a slog if you're still figuring out what a function is. Plus most ML jobs end up needing solid software engineering skills, so the foundation isn't wasted.

That said, if ML is what actually excites you, don't force yourself through months of CSS just because someone said to. Pick Python, do a basic intro to programming, then try a small ML project. You'll find out quickly if you like it.

My rough path would be: learn Python basics, build one small website or app (Flask or something simple), then try a beginner ML project like predicting house prices. Seeing both will tell you more than any advice here.

Whichever you pick, build things. Tutorials only get you so far.

Free apps make money in several ways, and most of them don't involve you paying directly.

**Advertising:** The most common method. Apps show you ads, and advertisers pay the app maker for views and clicks. Your usage data helps target those ads, which makes them more valuable.

**Freemium:** The basic app is free, but premium features cost money. Many people stick with the free version, but enough upgrade to cover the costs.

**In-app purchases:** Common in games. Players buy extra lives, cosmetic items, or currency. A small share of players, often called "whales," generate most of the revenue.

**Subscriptions:** A free trial leads into a monthly or yearly fee.

**Data:** Some apps collect and sell aggregated or anonymized user data to third parties. It's worth checking privacy policies.

**Other routes:** Sponsorships, affiliate commissions, selling merchandise, or using the app to promote a company's paid products or services. Some apps are also funded by investors who prioritize growth first and profit later.

The old saying applies: if you're not paying for the product, you may be the product.

Start by estimating your hours, then multiply by an hourly rate you'd be happy with. For a first project, a rate of $30-60/hour is common, depending on your skills and market. Add 25-50% padding to your estimate, because first projects almost always take longer than expected (revisions, unclear requirements, debugging).

Then quote a fixed price rather than hourly. Clients prefer certainty, and you'll earn more as you get faster.

Key tips:

- **Define scope in writing.** List pages, features, and number of revision rounds. Anything extra is a paid change request.
- **Take a deposit.** 30-50% upfront protects you and filters out unserious clients.
- **Break it into milestones** if the project is large.
- **Don't underprice drastically.** Very cheap work attracts difficult clients and is hard to raise later.
- **Ask about budget.** Sometimes the client already has a number in mind.

Track your actual hours afterward. That data will make your next quote far more accurate. Your first price won't be perfect, and that's fine. Treat it as learning, and raise your rates with each project.

It depends on the chatbot, the plan you're on, and what kind of data you're sharing.

**Check before you paste anything:**
- **Training policy:** Many free consumer tools may use your conversations to improve their models. Business or enterprise plans usually don't, and often say so in the contract.
- **Retention:** Find out how long chats are stored and whether you can delete them.
- **Security and compliance:** Look for encryption, access controls, and certifications like SOC 2 or ISO 27001. If you handle health, financial, or EU personal data, confirm HIPAA, GDPR, or similar compliance, and get a data processing agreement.
- **Company policy:** Your employer or clients may already have rules about this.

**Practical habits:**
- Never paste passwords, API keys, or customer personal information.
- Anonymize or remove names, account numbers, and identifiers.
- Use a paid business tier rather than a free personal account.
- Keep highly sensitive material, like trade secrets or legal matters, out of it unless your legal or security team approves.

In short, it can be safe with the right tool and precautions, but not by default.
